title: Half-lives and the random nature of radioactive decay

notes.definition: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time it takes for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample to halve, or the time it takes for the count rate (or activity) from a sample containing the isotope to fall to half its initial level.
explanation: Radioactive decay is random. You cannot predict when any one nucleus will decay; each unstable nucleus has the same chance of decaying in a given time. However, a sample contains a huge number of nuclei, so the overall pattern is very predictable. This is like throwing thousands of dice: you cannot say which will land on six, but you can predict that about one sixth will.

Because a fixed fraction of the remaining nuclei decays in each time interval, the number of undecayed nuclei falls by half in a fixed time, whatever amount you start with. This time is the half-life. It can be defined as the time for the number of nuclei of the isotope in a sample to halve, or as the time for the count rate (or activity) from the sample to fall to half its initial level. As the number of unstable nuclei falls, the activity falls too, because there are fewer nuclei left to decay.

To find a half-life from a graph of activity (or count rate) against time, choose a starting value, find half of that value, and read off the time taken to fall to it. The start does not have to be at time zero. It is good practice to repeat this from a different starting point and take a mean. The curve never quite reaches zero, but it gets closer and closer.

To calculate how much is left after a number of half-lives, keep halving: after 1 half-life ½ remains, after 2 half-lives ¼, after 3 half-lives ⅛ and so on. To find the number of half-lives, divide the total time by the half-life. For example, 800 Bq with a half-life of 2 days: after 6 days (3 half-lives) the activity is 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 Bq.

Count-rate measurements include background radiation. Before working out a half-life from real data, subtract the background count rate from each reading, so only the radiation from the source is used. Because decay is random, readings fluctuate, so a smooth curve of best fit is drawn through the points.
keyFacts: Radioactive decay is random: you cannot predict which nucleus will decay next, or when.
Half-life: time for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample to halve.
Half-life: also the time for the count rate or activity to fall to half its initial level.
The half-life of an isotope is constant, whatever the starting amount.
After n half-lives, the amount left = initial amount × (½)ⁿ.
Number of half-lives = time elapsed ÷ half-life.
Find the half-life from a graph by reading the time for any value to halve.
Subtract background count rate before using count rate data.
Activity falls over time because fewer unstable nuclei remain.

keyTerms.definition: The time for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample to halve, or for the count rate or activity to fall to half its initial level.
Impossible to predict for an individual nucleus; only the average behaviour of a large number can be predicted.
The rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays, in becquerels (Bq).
The number of decays recorded each second by a detector.
A graph of activity, count rate or number of undecayed nuclei against time; it falls by half every half-life.
The total fall in activity or count rate after a given time, often expressed as a ratio of the initial value.

equations.name: Amount remaining after n half-lives
equations.formula: amount remaining = initial amount × (½)ⁿ, where n = time ÷ half-life
equations.units: same units as initial amount (Bq, counts/s or number of nuclei)

workedExamples.title: Net decline as a ratio (Higher)
workedExamples.question: A source has an initial activity of 640 Bq. Calculate the net decline after 3 half-lives, as a ratio of the initial activity.
workedExamples.answer: 7 : 8 (the activity has fallen by ⅞ of its initial value)

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that after two half-lives all of the sample has decayed.
misconceptions.right: In fact half decays in the first half-life and half of the remainder in the second, so one quarter is left.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think half-life is half the time it takes for the whole sample to decay.
misconceptions.right: In fact a sample never fully decays in a predictable time; half-life is the time for the amount left to halve.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think we can predict which nucleus will decay next if we know the half-life.
misconceptions.right: In fact decay is random for individual nuclei; half-life describes the average behaviour of a large number.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often read the half-life as the time for the activity to fall by a fixed amount, such as 100 Bq.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is the time for the activity to halve, so the fall gets smaller each half-life (800 → 400 is a fall of 400; 400 → 200 is a fall of 200).

realWorld: Radiocarbon dating uses the 5700-year half-life of carbon-14 to work out the age of ancient organic remains.
Hospitals choose tracers with half-lives of a few hours so that the patient's body is not exposed to radiation for long.
Nuclear waste must be stored safely for many half-lives until its activity has fallen to a safe level.
higherTier: Determine the net decline, expressed as a ratio, in a radioactive emission after a given number of half-lives. After n half-lives the fraction remaining is (½)ⁿ, so the net decline is 1 − (½)ⁿ of the initial value. For example, after 2 half-lives the net decline is ¾ (a ratio of 3 : 4); after 3 half-lives it is ⅞ (7 : 8).
examTips: When reading a half-life from a graph, draw construction lines on the graph and show the halving clearly. Examiners award marks for them.
You can start at any point on the curve, not only at time zero.
Write out the halving chain (800 → 400 → 200) to avoid losing count of half-lives.
Subtract background count first if it is given, then halve.
Higher: make clear whether the question wants the fraction remaining (e.g. ¼) or the net decline (e.g. ¾).
summary: Radioactive decay is random for individual nuclei but predictable for large numbers.
Half-life is the time for the number of nuclei, activity or count rate to halve.
After n half-lives, (½)ⁿ of the original remains.
Read half-life from a graph by finding the time for any value to halve.
Higher: net decline after n half-lives is 1 − (½)ⁿ of the initial value, written as a ratio.

flashcards.front: What is meant by half-life (number of nuclei)?
flashcards.back: The time for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample to halve.

flashcards.front: What is meant by half-life (count rate)?
flashcards.back: The time for the count rate or activity to fall to half its initial level.

flashcards.front: Why is radioactive decay described as random?
flashcards.back: It is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay.

flashcards.front: How do you find the number of half-lives in a time?
flashcards.back: Divide the time by the half-life.

flashcards.front: How do you read half-life from a decay graph?
flashcards.back: Pick a value, find half of it, and read the time taken to fall to that value.

flashcards.front: Why does activity fall over time?
flashcards.back: There are fewer unstable nuclei left to decay.

flashcards.front: What should you do with background count before finding half-life?
Activity 400 Bq, half-life 1 h. Activity after 3 h?
Higher: net decline after 2 half-lives as a ratio?
flashcards.back: 3 : 4 (¾ of the initial activity has gone).

flashcards.back: No, it is constant for a given isotope.

questions.question: What is meant by the half-life of a radioactive isotope?
options: Half the time it takes for all the nuclei to decay
The time for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample to halve
The time for the mass number to halve
The time for a single nucleus to decay
markScheme: 1 mark: The time for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample to halve
questions.explanation: Half-life is the time for the number of unstable nuclei (or activity) to halve. A sample never completely decays in a predictable time.

questions.question: Why is radioactive decay described as random?
options: It is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay
Nuclei decay faster when heated
All nuclei decay at the same moment
Only some isotopes are radioactive
markScheme: 1 mark: It is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay
questions.explanation: Random means we cannot predict when any particular nucleus will decay. Temperature has no effect on decay.

questions.question: What fraction of a radioactive sample is left undecayed after 2 half-lives?
options: ½
⅛
¼
markScheme: 1 mark: ¼
questions.explanation: ½ × ½ = ¼. Two half-lives do not make the sample disappear.

questions.question: A source has an activity of 1200 Bq and a half-life of 6 hours. What is its activity after 18 hours?
options: 400 Bq
300 Bq
150 Bq
600 Bq
markScheme: 1 mark: 150 Bq
questions.explanation: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 half-lives: 1200 → 600 → 300 → 150 Bq. 400 Bq comes from dividing by 3 instead of halving three times.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how the activity of a radioactive source changes with time.
Use Figure 1 to determine the half-life of the source.
options: 5 days
7.5 days
3 days
15 days
markScheme: 1 mark: 5 days

questions.question: Which statement about half-life is correct?
options: Half-life gets shorter as the sample gets smaller
Half-life is the same whatever the size of the sample
Half-life is the time for the mass of the sample to halve
Half-life can be changed by heating the sample
markScheme: 1 mark: Half-life is the same whatever the size of the sample
questions.explanation: Half-life is a fixed property of an isotope. Note that the mass of the sample hardly changes, because the decayed nuclei become other nuclei.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how the activity of a radioactive sample changes with time.
Why does the activity of the sample decrease over time?
options: The nuclei decay more slowly as they get older
The radiation gets weaker as it travels
The half-life increases
There are fewer unstable nuclei left to decay
markScheme: 1 mark: There are fewer unstable nuclei left to decay
questions.explanation: Each unstable nucleus has the same chance of decaying per second. With fewer of them left, there are fewer decays each second.

questions.question:
The activity of a radioactive source is measured over 4 half-lives.
What is the net decline in activity, expressed as a ratio of the initial activity?
questions.explanation: After 4 half-lives, (½)⁴ = 1/16 remains, so 15/16 has declined: 15 : 16. 1 : 16 is the fraction remaining, not the decline.

questions.question: A student has a sample of 1 000 000 unstable nuclei. Which statement is correct?
options: Exactly 500 000 nuclei will decay in one half-life
The student can predict which nucleus will decay first
About 500 000 nuclei will decay in one half-life
All the nuclei will have decayed after two half-lives
markScheme: 1 mark: About 500 000 nuclei will decay in one half-life
questions.explanation: Decay is random, so the number decaying in one half-life is approximately, not exactly, half. With large numbers the result is very close to half.

questions.question:
A radioactive sample has an activity of 800 Bq.
The half-life of the sample is 3 hours.
Calculate the activity of the sample after 9 hours.
markScheme: 1 mark: 9 ÷ 3 = 3 half-lives
questions.explanation: Three halvings: 800 ÷ 8 = 100 Bq.

questions.question:
A sample contains 6.4 × 10⁶ unstable nuclei.
Calculate the number of unstable nuclei that remain after 4 half-lives.

Table 1 shows how the count rate from a radioactive source changes with time.
The background count rate has already been subtracted.
Use Table 1 to determine the half-life of the source.
markScheme: 1 mark: 480 halves to 240 (or 340 to 170, or 240 to 120)
1 mark: half-life = 20 minutes
questions.explanation: 480 → 240 takes 20 minutes. Check: 340 → 170 also takes 20 minutes, and 240 → 120 takes 20 minutes.

questions.question:
Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5700 years.
A piece of ancient wood contains ¼ of the carbon-14 found in living wood.
Calculate the age of the wood.
markScheme: 1 mark: ¼ means 2 half-lives
questions.explanation: Fraction ¼ = (½)², so 2 half-lives have passed: 11 400 years.

questions.question:
A radioactive source has a half-life of 4 days.
After 16 days the activity of the source is 50 Bq.
Calculate the initial activity of the source.
markScheme: 1 mark: 16 ÷ 4 = 4 half-lives
1 mark: 50 × 2⁴ = 800 Bq
questions.explanation: Work backwards by doubling 4 times: 50 → 100 → 200 → 400 → 800 Bq.

questions.question:
A radioactive source has an initial activity of 640 Bq.
Calculate the net decline in activity after 3 half-lives.
markScheme: 1 mark: activity after 3 half-lives = 640 ÷ 8 = 80 Bq
1 mark: net decline = 640 − 80 = 560 Bq
questions.explanation: The net decline is the total fall: initial minus final. As a ratio this is 560 : 640 = 7 : 8.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows measurements made with a detector placed near a radioactive source.
The half-life of the source is 10 minutes.
Calculate the count rate the detector will measure 20 minutes later.
markScheme: 1 mark: count rate from source = 820 − 20 = 800 counts/min
1 mark: after 2 half-lives source gives 800 ÷ 4 = 200 counts/min
1 mark: measured = 200 + 20 = 220 counts/min
questions.explanation: Only the source's count rate halves; background stays the same. A common error is halving 820 twice to get 205.

rows: Count rate measured by the detector now

questions.question:
A radioactive sample has an activity of 960 Bq.
The half-life of the sample is 5 years.
Calculate the time taken for the activity to fall to 60 Bq.
markScheme: 1 mark: 960 → 480 → 240 → 120 → 60 is 4 half-lives
1 mark: 4 × 5 = 20 years
questions.explanation: 960 ÷ 60 = 16 = 2⁴, so 4 half-lives, which is 20 years.

questions.question: Give the definition of half-life in terms of count rate.
acceptedAnswers: time for count rate to halve
fall to half its initial level
count rate to fall to half
markScheme: 1 mark: time taken for the count rate (or activity) to fall to half its initial level
questions.explanation: Either definition is accepted; this one uses count rate.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by saying that radioactive decay is random.
acceptedAnswers: cannot predict when a nucleus will decay
cannot predict which nucleus will decay next
markScheme: 1 mark: you cannot predict which nucleus will decay next
1 mark: or when a particular nucleus will decay
questions.explanation: Random applies to individual nuclei; large samples still show a predictable half-life.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how the activity of a radioactive isotope changes with time.
Describe how Figure 1 can be used to find the half-life of the isotope.
markScheme: 1 mark: choose an activity on the curve and find the time taken for it to fall to half that value
1 mark: draw construction lines / repeat from a different starting point and take a mean
questions.explanation: Construction lines and a repeat improve the reliability of the reading.

questions.question: A student says that a source with a half-life of 2 hours will have no activity after 4 hours. Explain why the student is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: 4 hours is 2 half-lives
1 mark: so ¼ of the activity remains (activity halves each half-life and never reaches zero in this way)
questions.explanation: Each half-life only halves what is left, so ½ × ½ = ¼ remains.

questions.question: Explain why the half-life of a sample is the same whatever the size of the sample.
acceptedAnswers: proportion decays per unit time constant
markScheme: 1 mark: each nucleus has the same chance (probability) of decaying in a given time
1 mark: so the same fraction (half) of any number decays in the same time
questions.explanation: The fraction decaying per unit time depends on the isotope, not on how many nuclei there are.

questions.question: A source has an initial count rate of 360 counts/s. Determine the net decline in count rate after 2 half-lives, expressed as a ratio of the initial count rate. Give your answer in its simplest form.
markScheme: 1 mark: count rate after 2 half-lives = 90 counts/s, so decline = 270 counts/s
1 mark: ratio 270 : 360 = 3 : 4
questions.explanation: After 2 half-lives ¼ remains, so ¾ has gone: 3 : 4.

questions.question: Explain why a student should subtract the background count rate from the readings before calculating a half-life.
markScheme: 1 mark: background radiation is not from the source / does not decay with the source's half-life
1 mark: so including it would give the wrong (too long) half-life
questions.explanation: Background stays roughly constant, so it would make the count rate appear to fall more slowly.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by half-life, and how the random nature of decay is linked to the idea of half-life.
markScheme: Indicative content: half-life is the time for the number of unstable nuclei to halve, or the time for count rate/activity to fall to half; decay is random, so you cannot predict when a particular nucleus will decay; each nucleus has the same probability of decaying in a given time; with very large numbers of nuclei the fraction decaying is predictable; so the number halves in a fixed time; half-life is constant for an isotope.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear definition and a logical link between randomness of individual decays and the predictable half-life of large samples.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): a definition or a statement about randomness, with little linking.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The key link: individual nuclei are unpredictable, but large numbers average out to a reliable halving time.

questions.question:
A scientist measures the count rate from a radioactive sample every hour.
Table 1 shows the results.
The background count rate is 30 counts/min.
Explain how the scientist should use the data in Table 1 to determine the half-life.
Determine the half-life and the net decline in the count rate from the source over the 4 hours, expressed as a ratio of its initial count rate.
markScheme: Indicative content: subtract background from each reading: 960, 480, 240, 120, 60 counts/min; plot corrected count rate against time and draw a smooth curve; read time for count rate to halve, e.g. 960 → 480 in 1 hour; repeat for other intervals (480 → 240, 240 → 120) and take a mean; half-life = 1 hour; 4 hours = 4 half-lives; final corrected count rate 60 = 960 ÷ 16; net decline = 960 − 60 = 900 counts/min; ratio 900 : 960 = 15 : 16; explain that randomness means real data fluctuate so a curve of best fit is used.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): background correctly subtracted, clear method, correct half-life of 1 hour and correct net decline ratio 15 : 16.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): background correction and half-life correct, or method described with a partly correct ratio.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some relevant steps, e.g. halving the raw data without correcting for background.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Using the raw data would wrongly suggest the half-life is longer than 1 hour (990 is not halved to 510 in exactly 1 hour). Corrected values halve exactly every hour.
